TECH · TechCrunch · editor 9/10 · 1 min read fact-checked

OpenAI Introduces Virtual Try-On and Favorites for ChatGPT Shopping

OpenAI has globally launched new shopping features for its conversational AI assistant, ChatGPT, on Thursday. These updates aim to enhance online retail experiences by allowing users to virtually try on clothing and accessories and save desired products for later.

The new functionalities leverage the ChatGPT Images 2.5 model, which OpenAI states offers more natural lighting, richer textures, reliable editing instructions, and reduced image generation latency. Users can upload a selfie or full-body photo to visualize items, or even upload an image of an item to have ChatGPT try it on for them. A new “try on” button appears in shopping results to facilitate this.

Alongside the virtual try-on, a new Favorites option enables users to save discovered products to a Library within the app, storing them with try-on images. These developments position ChatGPT in areas previously dominated by platforms like Pinterest and Google, which launched its own virtual try-on feature last year.

OpenAI's move follows earlier experimentation in the shopping space, including an instant checkout feature that did not perform well. The company is now focusing on consumer use cases that integrate its advanced AI image generation with practical shopping tools.

What to watch: How ChatGPT's new shopping features compete with existing retail visualization tools.

NATIONAL · News18 India · editor 9/10 · 1 min read fact-checked

India's Drug Panel Seeks Tighter Watch on Narcotic Medicines, States' Aid Against Fakes

India's Drugs Consultative Committee (DCC), at its 70th meeting on September 18, recommended a tighter system for tracking medicines containing narcotic and psychotropic substances. This initiative aims to curb the diversion of legally sold strong painkillers and sedatives into the illegal market, a concern outlined in the “Vision Document on Drug Control 2026 to 2029.”

The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) has been tasked to address regulatory gaps by March 2027. The expert panel stressed the need for a reliable national database covering manufacture, sale, stocking, inspections, and enforcement actions. States and union territories are expected to submit monthly reports detailing licenses issued, medicine handling, inspections conducted, and actions taken, with CDSCO finalizing the reporting format.

Additionally, the committee proposed a common digital platform for data submission and analysis, suggesting the adaptation of an existing Central Bureau of Narcotics portal for end-to-end tracking of these drugs from factory to shop. All these recommendations require approval from the Drug Controller General of India (DCGI) to take effect.

Separately, the DCC is pushing to combat fake medicines, following recommendations from the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC)'s open house on February 25. States and union territories will be circulated the NHRC recommendations for comments and details on current measures, paving the way for a combined proposal from CDSCO and coordinated action among various agencies.

What to watch: The DCGI's approval and implementation timeline for the proposed drug tracking system.

Russian President Vladimir Putin warned on Thursday that the world cannot be certain nuclear weapons will never be used, emphasizing the increasing risks associated with powerful armaments. Speaking at the Valdai Discussion Club forum in Moscow, Putin stated, “If a gun is hanging on the stage, sooner or later it must go off,” underscoring the potential for catastrophic global consequences from the leading powers' arsenals.

Putin cautioned that escalating conflicts could rapidly reach a point of no return, attributing this dangerous trajectory to “arrogance and overconfidence.” He urged countries to avoid such a fatal threshold, highlighting that the moment when changes become impossible may arrive unexpectedly.

His remarks coincided with heightened warnings from Moscow regarding the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, situated between NATO members Poland and Lithuania. Putin asserted that Russia would consider deploying “all weapons at its disposal” in the event of a direct attack on Kaliningrad or any other Russian territory.

While stating Russia has no plans to attack European countries and desires peaceful coexistence, Putin characterized NATO as an adversary larger than Russia. These comments come amidst ongoing tensions between Moscow and Western nations over the conflict in Ukraine.

SPORTS · NDTV Sports · editor 10/10 · 1 min read fact-checked

Nitesh Siwach Secures Historic Greco-Roman Silver at Asian Games 2026

Indian wrestler Nitesh Siwach clinched a silver medal at the Asian Games 2026, marking a significant achievement as only the second Indian to reach a Greco-Roman wrestling final at the continental showpiece. Competing in the men's 97 kg category, Siwach narrowly missed the gold, losing to Japan's Yuri Nakazato in the final at the Nagoya City Inae Sports Centre on Thursday.

His silver medal ended India's 64-year wait for a Greco-Roman wrestling finalist at the Asian Games, a feat last achieved by Maruti Mane at the 1962 Asian Games, who also won silver in the same weight category. Siwach dedicated his medal to his father, stating, “My father always told me there was no looking back once I started this journey, that I had to bring home a medal, and today, I did it for him.”

Siwach demonstrated strong performances in the knockout stages, defeating Turkmenistan's Amanberdi Agamammedov 7-1 in the quarterfinals and overpowering Mongolia's Ganbaataryn Gankhuyag 9-0 in the semifinal. Despite the pressure of being in a weight category with no prior Indian medalists, he trusted his training.

In the final, Nakazato secured a 2-0 lead after Siwach was penalized for passivity, extending it to 4-0 in the second period. Siwach, who arrived in Nagoya as a 2026 Asian Championships silver medallist, also expressed gratitude to the Inspire Institute of Sport for their comprehensive support. He added, "Maine apne desh ka Tiranga lehra diya."

What to watch: The continued development of Indian Greco-Roman wrestling talent.

Unlike other fusion fuels, hydrogen-boron reactions produce fewer radioactive byproducts, presenting a cleaner alternative for long-term energy generation. SCIENCE BRIEF · Phys.org · editor 9/10 · 1 min read fact-checked

Physicists Identify 'Singular Funnels' in Complex Systems

Researchers led by Serhiy Yanchuk have discovered 'singular funnels,' narrow pathways that allow complex systems to transition between stable states. Published in Physical Review Letters, the study explains how these structures enable systems to reach stability from starting points previously considered impossible by simpler models.

These funnels exist in systems ranging from basic models to linked oscillators. While these pathways narrow as the gap between fast and slow processes increases, they never fully disappear. This finding reveals that disturbances can trigger state switches in ways that conventional, simplified models fail to capture.

Researchers Develop Water-Soluble Glycopolymers Using 4-Trehalosamine

A research team led by Saitama University's Koji Matsuoka has utilized the microbial metabolite 4-trehalosamine to design a new platform for water-soluble glycopolymers. By leveraging the C4 amino group as a chemical handle, researchers successfully synthesized a polymerizable acrylamide monomer without needing to distinguish between multiple similar hydroxyl groups.

The study, published in Carbohydrate Research, confirms that this method allows for the creation of composition-tunable polyacrylamides. This approach simplifies the modification of sugar-based materials, combining the inherent biological properties of carbohydrates with the processability of synthetic polymers.

Bombay HC Rules WhatsApp Video Circulation Under SC/ST Act

The Bombay High Court has ruled that circulating a video of a person belonging to the Scheduled Caste/Scheduled Tribe (SC/ST) community on WhatsApp falls within “public view” and attracts provisions of the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act. Justice Yanshivraj Khobragade delivered this ruling while dismissing a bail plea.

The appellant, Nikhil Thepale, is accused of demanding favours from a victim from the SC/ST community. When the victim refused, Thepale recorded videos and photographs of her, subsequently sending them on WhatsApp to her husband, sister-in-law, and other relatives.

Thepale faces charges under Sections 77 and 78 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Sections 66(E) and 67 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, and Sections 3(1)(r) and 3(1)(w)(ii) of the Atrocities Act. The FIR was lodged on November 5, 2025, and Thepale has been absconding since that date, a factor Justice Khobragade cited in denying bail.

What to watch: The ruling clarifies legal implications for digital content sharing involving SC/ST individuals.

No UPI Day Protest Called Off: What This Means for Your Payments

The proposed ‘No UPI Day’ protest, planned for October 2 (Gandhi Jayanti), has been called off. This means consumers can expect normal UPI payment services at mobile retailers and other participating businesses, as the All India Mobile Retailers Association (AIMRA) and the All India Consumer Products Distributors Federation (AICPDF) have withdrawn their protest.

The protest was organized to oppose a new 0.4% UPI Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) set to apply from October 15, 2026, on specified merchant transactions exceeding ₹2,000. This charge is levied on the merchant, not directly on the customer, and retailers expressed concerns that it would add pressure to their already thin profit margins.

Following a meeting with Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, the trade delegation, led by BJP MP Praveen Khandelwal and AIMRA founder Kailash Lakhyani, sought a deferment of the MDR, a phased implementation starting at 0.20% in 2026-27, and an increase in the applicability threshold from ₹1 lakh to ₹5 lakh. Sitharaman assured them that their concerns would be addressed, leading to the protest's withdrawal.

SCIENCE · Phys.org · editor 9/10 · 1 min read fact-checked

New Research Reveals Distinctive Deepfake Victim-Blaming for Celebrities

New research led by Irish researchers has identified distinctive forms of victim-blaming, harassment, and barriers to justice faced by celebrity victim-survivors of deepfake sexual abuse. The study, published in the International Journal of Human-Computer Studies, is the first to pinpoint deepfake-specific victim-blaming and harm-minimizing myths within these experiences.

The research found that victims endure significant psychological, emotional, social, and reputational harm. They often face claims that deepfake images are "not harmful" because they are fake, or that public figures should "expect" such content. This study, led by researchers at University College Cork (UCC) and the University of Limerick (UL), highlights how these myths exacerbate harm and fuel online harassment. Dr. John Twomey, who led the research as part of his Ph.D. at UCC and is now an assistant professor at UL, noted that speaking out can come at a "real cost," with advocates risking further deepfake content.

Celebrities face a dilemma: raising awareness can expose them to more harassment. Many remain silent fearing permanent association with sexually explicit deepfakes or driving more searches for abusive imagery. The study also details major barriers to removal and justice, including time-consuming reporting processes with limited results and difficulty identifying perpetrators. Professor Gillian Murphy of UCC, a study supervisor, emphasized the need for responses that lessen the burden on victims and challenge the notion that fabricated images are less harmful.

What to watch: Future policy discussions on deepfake regulation and victim support.

SCIENCE · Phys.org · editor 10/10 · 1 min read fact-checked

Alaska's Permafrost Soils Warming Rapidly, Posing Climate and Infrastructure Risks

New research from Washington State University reveals that Alaska's soils are warming quickly and at considerable depth, with the fastest increases occurring in the state's permafrost region. This trend, documented between 1997 and 2023, could accelerate climate change by releasing carbon dioxide and methane as permafrost thaws, and also undermine the stability of crucial infrastructure like roads and buildings.

The study, published in Frontiers in Climate, synthesized air and soil temperature data from 43 weather stations across Alaska over 27 years. It found that air temperatures in permafrost regions rose at 1.15 degrees Celsius per decade, while soil temperatures increased at 0.64 degrees Celsius per decade. Lead author Erin Oliver, a postdoctoral research associate at WSU, noted that soil warming rates were not slowing deeper in the soil; in fact, 100% of weather stations in the permafrost region showed a warming trend at a depth of 4 feet (1.2 meters).

Winter snow cover plays a key role, with deeper snow at lower latitudes slowing warming rates. In the permafrost region, most warming occurred in winter, while lower latitudes experienced more summer warming, which could impact growing seasons. Co-author Claire Phillips, a WSU research soil scientist, highlighted the "upsetting" finding of 2 to 3 degrees Celsius per decade warming at 4 feet depth during winter months in permafrost soils.

What to watch: Policy and planning responses to permafrost thaw and its implications for Alaskan communities.

Source: Phys.org · permalink · more science

FINANCE · Livemint Money · editor 9/10 · 1 min read fact-checked

Indian Household Debt Growth Outpaces Asset Accumulation in 2025

Indian households experienced a notable trend in 2025, where their liabilities grew significantly faster than their financial assets, according to the Allianz Global Wealth Report 2026. Household borrowing climbed by 14.3% during the year, reaching $1.59 trillion. In contrast, gross financial assets increased by 9%, totaling $5.3 trillion.

For the ordinary saver, this means that while savings and investments continued to accumulate, a larger portion of this new wealth was offset by increased debt. Consequently, net financial assets, which account for liabilities, expanded by just 6.8% in 2025. This rate was lower than the growth of gross financial assets and diverged from the global trend, where worldwide liabilities rose by only 3.4% against an 8.6% increase in financial assets.

Despite this, Indian households have seen substantial long-term wealth creation. After adjusting for inflation, financial assets were 57% higher in 2025 compared to 2019. Within their portfolios, deposits continue to dominate, accounting for 40.2% of total financial assets, followed by securities at 32.7% and life insurance and pension assets at 26.7%. Insurance and pension assets recorded the strongest growth at 11.4% in 2025.

What to watch: The ongoing balance between household borrowing and asset growth in future reports.

Source: Livemint Money · permalink · more finance

This initiative is expected to benefit lakhs of women who contribute significantly to agri-food systems, livestock, poultry, and fisheries but are often excluded from formal farmer definitions.

The move addresses the growing feminization of agriculture, where women increasingly manage agricultural lands as men seek non-farm employment. Despite their heightened responsibilities, these women frequently lack corresponding control, assets, or decision-making power. Without land titles, they face significant barriers in accessing crucial resources such as credit, water, technology, and extension services, essentially reducing them to laborers in the sector they sustain.

Nationally, women constitute nearly 60% of the agricultural workforce, as reported by the Periodic Labour Force Survey and the Union Minister of State for Agriculture, Ramnath Thakur, yet hold less than 15% of land titles. In Maharashtra specifically, 82% of the rural female workforce is involved in agriculture, but women possess only about 15.5% of operational farmland, highlighting the local relevance and urgency of this new legislation.

The Microfluidics Cluster EHU research group, led by Ikerbasque research professor Lourdes Basabe-Desmonts, engineered this discreet and portable tool. The research is published in the journal *Talanta*.

Poves emphasized that the device aims to prevent drug-facilitated assault by enabling quick onsite detection before ingestion, addressing the limitations of traditional laboratory-dependent analytical techniques. This development is part of a larger project by the Microfluidics Cluster UPV/EHU group to create a single microfluidic platform capable of detecting multiple drugs, with a similar device for benzodiazepines already developed. Researchers note it is currently a laboratory-level prototype requiring further refinement.

On 24 April 1890, more than 10,000 mill workers gathered at the Race Course Ground in Mahalaxmi, Bombay, to demand a weekly day of rest. This movement marked the beginning of a long-term shift in the relationship between the Indian state, employers, and the industrial workforce.

Decades later, these early labor efforts culminated in the Employees' Provident Funds Act of 1952. The scheme expanded in stages to cover major industries including textiles, cement, and engineering. Today, the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) manages the retirement savings of approximately 7.98 crore contributing members and oversees assets exceeding Rs 25 lakh crore. The system now provides a comprehensive safety net, including pensions and insurance, while allowing partial withdrawals for education, marriage, and housing. These scans offer detailed insights into bone structure and recovery status, helping mitigate the risk of injury from premature physical exertion. The study underscores the need for preventive measures, including targeted drugs, exercise, and dietary adjustments, to preserve astronauts’ baseline skeletal health before and after missions.

Regional Legal Hurdles Stall Response to Indonesian Transboundary Haze

Persistent haze from Indonesian wildfires has impacted Malaysia and Singapore for over a month, causing school closures and rising respiratory health issues. Legal experts note that neighboring nations lack viable recourse via the International Court of Justice due to jurisdictional requirements and a lack of mutual consent. While the three nations are signatories to the 2002 ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution, the treaty lacks litigation mechanisms, favoring consensus and non-interference over enforcement. Experts suggest that regional cooperation on hotspot monitoring and information sharing remains the most practical path forward, as private lawsuits against companies linked to illegal burning face significant evidentiary challenges in Indonesian courts.
